title: Psychology · Episode 3
chapters: Cognitive dissonance: why we twist the facts to feel better

units.t: Psychology. Episode three.
In this episode: Cognitive dissonance: why we twist the facts to feel better, Why we procrastinate and The psychology of persuasion.
Part one. Cognitive dissonance: why we twist the facts to feel better.
When reality clashes with what we believe or what we've done, something has to give.
Surprisingly often, it isn't the belief.
A prophecy fails.
In 1954, a small group in the American Midwest believed a flood would destroy much of the world on 21 December, and that a flying saucer would rescue the faithful beforehand.
Some members quit jobs and gave away possessions.
Unknown to the group, several new members were researchers working with psychologist Leon Festinger.
They watched as midnight passed with no spaceship and no flood.
Rather than abandon the belief, the leader announced that the group's faith had saved the world, and some members began seeking publicity and recruits for the first time.
Festinger and colleagues described the episode in the 1956 book When Prophecy Fails.
It illustrated an idea Festinger would soon make famous.
What dissonance is.
In 1957 Festinger published A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance.
When we hold two beliefs, or a belief and an action, that conflict, we feel an uncomfortable tension.
A smoker who knows smoking kills experiences it every time they light up.
That discomfort motivates us to restore consistency, and there are only a few ways.
We can change our behaviour, by quitting.
We can change our belief, by deciding the risks are exaggerated.
Or we can add thoughts that soften the clash, such as 'my grandfather smoked and lived to ninety' or 'everyone dies of something'.
Changing behaviour is often the hardest option, so the mind quietly reaches for the others.
Justifying our choices.
Dissonance is thought to be strongest after a hard decision.
If you agonised between two similar cars and bought one, you may suddenly notice how good your choice is and how flawed the other was.
In 1956 Jack Brehm had people choose between two appliances they liked equally; the chosen item tended to rise in their ratings, the rejected one to fall.
Later researchers noted a statistical problem with this design, and corrected studies often find a smaller effect.
In a 1968 racetrack study, punters who had just placed a bet were more confident of winning.
The same logic gives effort justification.
In a 1959 study, Elliot Aronson and Judson Mills found that people who endured an embarrassing initiation rated a dull group more highly.
It helps explain fierce loyalty after hazing, and why people stay with failing projects.
Debates and doubts.
The most famous dissonance study is a 1959 experiment by Festinger and James Carlsmith.
Students did an hour of dull tasks, then were paid one dollar or twenty to tell the next participant it was fun.
The one dollar group later rated the task as more enjoyable.
The explanation: twenty dollars was reason enough to lie, one dollar was not, so they decided the task wasn't so bad.
Replications of this kind of finding have been mixed, so it deserves caution.
The theory has always had critics.
In the 1960s Daryl Bem argued that we simply infer our attitudes from our behaviour.
Others suggested the real driver is protecting our self-image as a good, sensible person.
The doomsday study is also questioned.
Most psychologists still accept that people often rationalise, but treat specific classic experiments cautiously.
Using dissonance wisely.
The practical value of dissonance theory is self-awareness.
When you feel defensive, irritated or eager to explain something away, a cherished belief may have met an inconvenient fact.
Pausing to ask 'what would change my mind?'
helps.
So does separating your identity from your opinions: being wrong about a decision does not make you foolish.
In relationships, remember that others feel dissonance too, so cornering someone with evidence often makes them dig in.
Offering a face-saving way to change their mind works better.
There is a famous anecdote from Benjamin Franklin, who said he won over a rival by asking to borrow a rare book.
Helping you, perhaps, made the rival like you more.
The key idea: A doomsday group whose prophecy failed gave psychologists a view of how people defend a belief.
Part two. Why we procrastinate.
Procrastination isn't laziness or poor time management.
It's an emotion problem, and that's good news.
An emotion problem.
Around one in five adults describe themselves as chronic procrastinators, and nearly everyone does it sometimes.
It's tempting to blame laziness or poor organisation, but research by psychologists such as Tim Pychyl and Fuschia Sirois suggests otherwise.
Procrastination is mostly about emotions.
We delay tasks that make us feel bored, anxious, confused, overwhelmed or insecure, because putting them off gives instant relief.
That's a short-term fix with a long-term cost, and the relief rewards the delay, turning it into a habit.
The good news is that an emotion problem can be worked on.
Why we delay.
Economists call it present bias: rewards now feel much bigger than rewards later, so a finished report next week can't compete with scrolling right now.
Brain-imaging studies even find that thinking about our future selves looks more like thinking about a stranger, so we hand future-us the hard work as if it were somebody else's problem.
Perfectionism adds fuel.
Many procrastinators care a lot.
If a task feels like a test of your ability, starting risks proving you're not good enough, and delay protects your self-image with a ready excuse: 'I only did badly because I left it too late.'
Lower the stakes of starting.
Allow a terrible first draft, 'version zero'.
Perfection is for the end, never the beginning.
Make starting tiny.
Dread is usually worst before you begin, and it often fades once you start.
So make starting tiny: commit to two minutes, one paragraph, or just opening the document and writing the heading.
You may stop after that, but you often won't, partly because unfinished tasks tend to stay on your mind.
Even if you stop, you've broken the avoidance loop.
Make tasks concrete too.
'Do tax' or 'Plan the wedding' is vague, so your brain can't picture the first step.
Turn it into a next action that starts with a verb: 'Find last year's tax return', 'Email three venues for quotes'.
Productivity writer David Allen calls this the 'next action'.
Small steps feel less threatening and build momentum.
Time and surroundings.
Willpower is unreliable, especially when you're tired, so shape your time and surroundings instead.

The Pomodoro Technique, created by Francesco Cirillo in the late 1980s and named after a tomato-shaped kitchen timer, means 25 minutes on one task, then a 5-minute break, with a longer break after four rounds.
A deadline 25 minutes away is easy to face, and the break is a reward.
Timeboxing goes further: put the task in your calendar like an appointment, removing one more decision.
Then design out distraction.
Put your phone in another room, since just having it within reach invites a quick check.
Use website blockers, close extra tabs, work somewhere you associate with focus, and tell someone what you'll finish by when.
Forgive yourself.
Beating yourself up feels like it should help, but it usually makes things worse, because guilt is another unpleasant feeling to avoid.
In a study of university students, those who forgave themselves for procrastinating before their first exam procrastinated less before the next one.
Self-compassion isn't letting yourself off the hook; it's treating yourself like a friend who stumbled.
Acknowledge it, work out what made the task feel hard, and choose the next small step.
Then take it.
The key idea: Procrastination is mainly about avoiding unpleasant feelings, not poor time management.
Part three. The psychology of persuasion.
Most attempts to persuade you pull on the same few levers.
Once you see them, you can't unsee them.
The levers of yes.
In 1984, psychologist Robert Cialdini published Influence after studying salespeople, fundraisers and advertisers, even taking jobs undercover to learn their techniques.
He found that most persuasion relies on a handful of principles that trigger fairly automatic responses.
These shortcuts usually serve us well: following experts or returning favours is often sensible.
The trouble is that anyone who knows the shortcuts can trigger them on purpose.
In 2016 he added a seventh principle, unity, which appears later in this lesson.
Knowing the principles helps you persuade honestly and notice when someone is pushing your buttons.
Give, then ask.
Reciprocity is a deep social rule: we feel obliged to return favours, even for an uninvited gift.
Free supermarket samples, a 'complimentary' drink before a sales pitch and charity letters with a small gift all rely on it.
Restaurants that bring mints with the bill tend to get slightly bigger tips.
Consistency works alongside it.
Once we commit to something, especially publicly or in writing, we want to act consistently.
Salespeople use the 'foot in the door': get a small yes, like signing a petition or starting a free trial, and a bigger yes becomes more likely.
The defence isn't refusing every gift.
It's accepting without feeling you owe.
You can use consistency yourself: writing down a goal or telling a friend makes you likelier to follow through.
Crowds and experts.
When we're unsure, we look at what others are doing.
That's why a busy restaurant beats an empty one, and why reviews, star ratings and 'bestseller' labels work.
In one well-known hotel study, a card saying most guests reused their towels beat a card about saving the environment.
Social proof is strongest when the people are similar to us, but crowds can be wrong, and fake reviews and bought followers exploit this instinct.
Authority works similarly: we follow credible experts and also the symbols of expertise, such as uniforms, titles and lab coats.
Ads feature people who look like doctors or scientists for a reason.
Ask two questions: is this person truly an expert in this topic, and do they gain if I agree?
Liking, scarcity, unity.
We say yes more easily to people we like, and we like people who are similar to us, pay us compliments and cooperate with us.
That's why salespeople look for common ground, 'You're from Brisbane too?'
, and why products are sold through friends at parties.
Unity goes further: we're more easily influenced by people we see as part of 'us', such as family, a team or a hometown.
Scarcity makes things seem more valuable when they're rare or running out: 'Only 3 left', 'offer ends tonight'.
It ties to loss aversion, since missing out feels like losing something, and it cuts your thinking time.
Treat urgency as a signal to slow down.
Genuine bargains rarely vanish overnight, and a seller who won't let you sleep on it is telling you something.
Persuading honestly.
All seven principles can be used honestly.
If you give something first, show real reviews, cite real expertise, offer genuine value and set a true deadline, you're persuading ethically.
The line is crossed when the pressure is manufactured: fake scarcity, bought reviews, borrowed authority.
When you're on the receiving end, separate the person from the deal.
Would this offer still look good if a stranger you didn't warm to were making it?
And for your own persuasion, try a simple test: would you be comfortable if the other person knew exactly what you were doing?
Knowing the levers protects you from them and makes you a more honest persuader.
The key idea: Robert Cialdini found that most persuasion relies on a few principles that trigger fairly automatic responses.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What did the failed doomsday prophecy illustrate?
Answer. People may defend a belief harder when reality contradicts it.
Question two. According to the research, what is procrastination mostly about?
Answer. Avoiding unpleasant emotions like boredom.
Question three. Why can anyone use persuasion principles to trigger a yes on purpose?
Answer. They trigger quick shortcuts that usually serve us well.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
